blocks.content: The Cluster Autoscaler operates at a level above both HPA and VPA entirely, it adjusts the number of nodes in the cluster itself, not Pods, working directly with the cloud provider to add or remove real machines.
1. Adjusting Node Count, Not Pod Count
blocks.text: 1. Adjusting Node Count, Not Pod Count

blocks.content: This is a genuinely different level of scaling from everything else covered in this module, HPA and VPA both operate on Pods, the Cluster Autoscaler operates on the cluster's underlying compute itself, the worker nodes covered in the Architecture module.

blocks.alt: A different level entirely, scaling the underlying infrastructure, not the Pods on it

blocks.content: The Cluster Autoscaler watches for Pods stuck in the Pending phase, covered in the Pod Phases topic, specifically because the scheduler cannot find any node with enough free capacity to place them, when it sees this, it adds a new node.

blocks.alt: A real, observable signal, Pods that genuinely cannot be placed anywhere

blocks.content: The reverse happens as well, when a node is genuinely underutilized and its workloads could be safely consolidated elsewhere, the Cluster Autoscaler removes it, keeping the cluster's actual footprint, and cost, matched to real demand.

blocks.alt: Cost and footprint kept honest, not just capacity added and never reclaimed

blocks.content: 4. Working Through the Cloud Provider's API
blocks.text: 4. Working Through the Cloud Provider's API

blocks.content: Adding or removing a real node means actually provisioning or deprovisioning a real cloud machine, this happens through the cloud provider's own API, exactly the territory the Cloud Controller Manager, covered in the Architecture module, already operates in.

blocks.alt: Real infrastructure changes, made through the same cloud API territory covered earlier

blocks.content: 5. Three Autoscalers, Three Genuinely Different Levels
blocks.text: 5. Three Autoscalers, Three Genuinely Different Levels

blocks.content: Put together with HPA and VPA, this gives a complete picture: HPA scales Pod count, VPA scales individual Pod size, and Cluster Autoscaler scales the node count underneath all of it, three distinct, complementary levers.

blocks.alt: Three genuinely distinct levers, working at three different levels of the stack

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: The Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the cluster's actual node count, adding nodes when Pods are stuck Pending due to insufficient capacity, removing underutilized ones.
It works through the cloud provider's own API, the same territory as the Cloud Controller Manager, and together with HPA and VPA covers scaling at every level.
